course_details.Overview of class: How do children achieve the remarkable feat of acquiring language - an accomplishment we often take for granted? Which aspects of the human capacity for language are best understood as biological, as species-wide and species-specific? How do families, schools, and communities help shape children's development as speakers and listeners, and eventually as readers and writers? How does learning a first language (or more than one language) interact with learning to think, learning to imagine, and developing a sense of identity? To explore these questions, we will consider studies of children's language development along with perspectives from social policy, medicine, education, business and marketing, the arts and publishing. Students will have regular opportunities to reflect on their own experience, and each student will be able to select a topic of individual interest for a final seminar project. All assigned reading will be available to students on Canvas.
course_details.Registration Requirements: First-Year Seminar: WCAS First-Year Seminar; P/N Options: No P/N option for this section.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
By the end of this course, students should be able to:
• Pose questions. Formulate thoughtful and engaged questions and comments in seminar discussions. Pose questions about topics related to course content in written assignments, and motivate the importance and relevance of these questions.
• Find evidence. Identify main arguments and evidence in texts; summarize and evaluate arguments made by others. Identify relevant and reliable evidence to support claims.
• Make arguments. Formulate organized arguments based on careful analysis of evidence.
• Develop your voice. Select language appropriate for persuading specific audiences. Demonstrate progress in writing effectively at the college level.
• Cite sources appropriately.
course_details.Teaching Method: Discussion: Regular opportunities to write and to share ideas based on course readings and developed through writing.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Reaction papers, essays, participation in class discussion, short presentation.

course_details.Overview of class:
In LING 222 - SLAVIC 222 Language, Politics, and Identity (co-listed classes) students will examine and analyze political and identity issues in terms of the languages and dialects of the Balkans (particularly: Albanian, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Croatian, Macedonian, Romani, and Serbian). Topics to be covered include: linguistic nationalism, language laws, rights of minority languages, language discrimination, language and religion, alphabet issues, language and dialect as ethnic identity, standard language, and others. This course will introduce the student to some of the key issues that have plagued the Balkans in the past and continue to shape its future.
This course fulfills either an Area IV, Historical Studies, Distribution Requirement or Area V, Ethics and Values, Distribution Requirement, students may choose with Distribution Requirement.
course_details.Registration Requirements:
WCAS Distribution Requirement: Ethics & Values Distro Area
Historical Studies
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Describe the major historical events and figures within the Balkans, relevant to our sociolinguistic lens, from antiquity to modernity that have shaped key arguments about nationalism, language, and language-related social practices.
Intercept secondary sources (written histories, historical atlases of the Balkans, and other scholarly works) to acquire knowledge of the impact of historical developments and factors on the emergence and development of literary languages.
Apply a sociolinguistic social justice lens to these historical developments and factors, including the ancient civilizations (Illyria and Thrace) and major empires in the Balkans (Roman, Greek, Habsburg, and especially Ottoman), the decline of the Ottoman Empire and influx of Romantic nationalism, Communism, the Yugoslav Wars, and the rise of the European Union.
Analyze primary sources to discover the forms, effects, and causes of linguistic nationalism through the historical context. Primary texts include the 1850 Literary Agreement in Vienna, the 1954 Novi Sad Agreement, the 1967 Declaration on the Name and Position of the Croatian Literary Language, the 1974 revised Yugoslav Constitution, the 2017 Declaration on the Common Language, the 1944 Presidium of Anti-fascist Assembly of the National Liberation of Macedonia Announcement of Instruction in Schools in the Macedonian Language, the 1945 Foundation of the Macedonian Literary Language, and the 1945 People's Government of Macedonia Decree on the Macedonian Alphabet.
Reflect on the historical construction of ethnicity and nationalism and the roles these play in attitudes towards and policies concerning linguistic varieties (languages and dialects) and how they have changed over time. Particular attention will be given to the Ottoman Empire's administrative community structure, millet, in contrast to the Western Romantic nationalism entering the Balkans in the 19th century through external Western powers. Students will examine how these competing frameworks shaped and reshaped ethnicity and nationalism, ultimately contributing to forms of linguistic prejudice that have characterized the Balkans since the nineteenth century.
Recognize the significant symbolic role that language plays in politics and identity by describing and critiquing models of language policy within the Balkans ranging from total support and flourishing to attempting to kill and erase languages (and, consequently, peoples and cultures). Recognize the complexity of ethical issues associated with language politics and describe possible improvements to linguistic policy models based on the Balkan cases.
Identify linguistic prejudice through the myths and presuppositions about language (e.g., "speakers of African American English are verbally deprived"; "some languages are not good enough"; "everyone has an accent except me;" "French is a logical language"; "the meanings of words should not be allowed to change").
Discuss ways to prevent the perpetuation of linguistic prejudice and to promote linguistic justice and diversity within societies, particularly in contexts involving minority languages, colonization, genocide, and war.
Define foundational concepts of sociolinguistics/linguistic anthropology, using the Balkans as our primary case study and drawing comparisons with parallel US situations. Concepts include dialect continuum, language and identity, diglossia, alphabet reform, polycentric language models, language loss, language codification, language planning, and models of minority languages.
Discuss the vast and complex diachronic and synchronic multilayered diversity of the Balkans. Learn the countries and regions (historical, current, and non-existent, e.g., Greater Albania, non-territorial communities of Roma and Jews), major peoples and religions, and the names and genetic classifications of the major linguistic varieties (languages and dialects) while examining how these categories and systems of thought and speech have been constructed over time and space.
Communicate effectively about language policy and language politics in the Balkans and their historical development, expressing ideas thoughtfully and clearly in both oral and written forms.
Practice and improve group-work skills, including developing intercultural competence, sharing and supporting expertise, managing conflict within groups, planning and managing time effectively, giving and receiving constructive feedback, strengthening communication and listening skills, improving turn-taking practices, and holding oneself and others accountable.

course_details.Overview of class: In this class we will explore the formal structure of words (morphology) and sentences (syntax) in natural language. We will analyze data from a variety of languages (including English), focusing on the differences among morphological and syntactic systems, but also on the generalizations that can be made about all languages.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
By the end of this course, students should be able to:

1. Create and analyze formal models of the structure of words and sentences, accounting for regularities within and across languages.

2. Communicate arguments about word and sentence structure through graphical formats (tree diagrams), using empirical evidence and logical arguments to back claims.

3. Describe the advantages of applying similar formal constructs to a range of different linguistic structures within and across languages.

4. Explain the overarching questions addressed by the study of syntax and morphology, and describe the research areas targeted by other subfields in linguistics. Define basic terminology in linguistics, syntax, and morphology.

course_details.Overview of class: People use language to convey information. What makes a language suitable for this purpose, and how does it work? This question is at the center of the study of linguistic meaning. In this course, we will consider questions like these: How do the meanings of words like "everyone", "a", "hit", and "saw", give rise to the similarities and differences between "Everyone saw a hit," "Everyone hit a saw," "A saw hit everyone", etc.? Can we always tell for sure what a given sentence means, and does it mean the same on all occasions? Does meaning come from sentences or from a speaker's use of sentences? What are the different types of meaning (e.g., linguistic, contextual, social)? What's the place of meaning in an overall theory of language? We will explore a variety of approaches to these questions and discuss their theoretical assumptions, methodological tools, and empirical strengths and weaknesses. LING 270 satisfies the WCAS Area II (Formal Studies) Distribution Requirement and the Empirical and Deductive Reasoning Foundational Discipline (FD-EDR) Requirement.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
-Students will identify how humans express meaning
-Students will distinguish various kinds of linguistic meaning (including entailment, implicature, and presupposition)
-Students will analyze meaning in terms of a logical framework

course_details.Overview of class: Topic: French Phonetics. This course is designed to help you improve the pronunciation, intonation, and fluency of your spoken French, as well as to give you an overall understanding of the phonetic system of the contemporary French language.
course_details.Learning Objectives: The goal of the course is the development of native-like spoken French, through intense practice in correct production of the sounds of the language. Emphasis will be placed on intonation patterns, rhythm, liaison, etc. Oral practice is given within a communicative and cultural context, with attention to features of current usage referring to standard French. The course will also address issues in theoretical phonetics, particularly articulatory description and phonetic transcriptions using the International Phonetic Alphabet.
course_details.Teaching Method: The teaching method consists of lectures and discussions with numerous exercises geared towards specific problems, of extensive use of songs and poetry that reflect different registers of language, both formal and casual, and recordings of texts on a computer. Classes will be conducted exclusively in French.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Students will be evaluated based on their participation, oral and written homework, quizzes and exams, and a final oral exam.

course_details.Overview of class: This course engages with a variety of theoretical frameworks and analytic methods in sociolinguistics. The course will emphasize classic and contemporary work in linguistic variation and change, examining how this variation can reflect social structures, construct diverse social identities, and allow us to make sense of our surrounding social landscapes. We will discuss how quantitative methods in linguistics can be coupled with insights from linguistic anthropology and sociology to engage questions about the social conditioning of linguistic variation, language change, stylistic practice, and the connection between smaller-scale interactions and macro-social patterns of variation. We will also will examine how ideologies about linguistic variation have been used to invalidate particular ways of speaking and disempower speakers of these varieties, exploring the ways that language can reflect, reinforce, or ultimately contest social inequalities.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Prerequisites: graduate students, any 200-level Linguistics course, or consent of instructor
course_details.Learning Objectives: Through successfully completing this course, you will understand fundamental theoretical approaches to the study of sociolinguistics, become familiar with a variety of an analytic methods in sociolinguistic variation, and be able to connect the study of variation with social theoretic perspectives on structure, practice, and ideology. You will also be able to understand and critique the ways in which linguistic variation, change, and our ideologies surrounding language relate to social structures of power and inequality.

course_details.Overview of class: The course is a data-driven introduction to syntactic analysis. Through weekly writing assignments and in-class discussion, students will learn the analytical methods used in syntactic research: how to analyze syntactic data, how to formulate plausible hypotheses to explain the data, and how to compare and evaluate hypotheses. By the end of the course, students will have a fairly sophisticated knowledge of central properties of syntax. The course will introduce the students to and primarily operate within the government and binding framework of syntactic analysis, but we will cover alternative generative and non-generative approaches as well. Some of the specific topics covered by this course include phrase structure, head movement, A-movement, case and agreement, argument structure, binding, and locality constraints. Although the primary source of linguistic data will be English, examples will also be drawn from other languages both in class and on the writing assignments.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Pre-requisite: LING 260 or consent of the instructor.
course_details.Learning Objectives: This syntax course is geared toward fostering the acquisition of certain syntactic tools for analysis of complex linguistic patterns. Learning goals include: (1) Learning how to relate linguistic theory to natural language data; (2)Theory-building, starting with a limited set of assumptions and via analysis of complex linguistic patterns; (3)Figuring out and testing predictions of this theoretical system using analytical and experimental tools.

course_details.Overview of class: This course focuses on theoretical and practical issues in data visualization and the application of regression models to data in language science. You will use the statistical computing environment R to develop reproducible workflows for visualizing and statistically analyzing real data sets (e.g., acoustic measures, reaction times, error rates, scalar judgments), examining various levels of language structure (from sound to meaning), while accounting for variation across trials, participants, and items.
course_details.Registration Requirements: Prerequisites: One course in statistics (e.g., STAT 330), providing knowledge of basic descriptive statistics, significance tests of group differences (e.g., Z and t-tests), and correlation, or permission.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
By the end of class, students should be able to:
- Use appropriate quantitative or qualitative research methodologies to observe, describe, understand, and predict human behavior.
- Articulate the power and the limitations of statistical reasoning.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): Winter, B. Statistics for Linguists: An Introduction Using R. ISBN 9781138056091.
